Alexandria. Founded by Alexander the Great in three hundred thirty-two BCE on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, it became the intellectual and commercial capital of the Hellenistic world. Home to the legendary Library of Alexandria and the Pharos lighthouse—one of antiquity's Seven Wonders—it remained a beacon of learning, trade, and cultural exchange under the Ptolemaic dynasty and later Roman rule.

Alexander founded the city strategically after his conquest of Egypt. He chose a defensible natural harbor at the mouth of the Nile River. Following Alexander's death, Alexandria became the capital of Egypt under the Ptolemaic dynasty, replacing the ancient inland capital of Memphis and establishing a new Hellenistic center. Named in honor of Alexander and intentionally designed as a cosmopolitan Greek city, it blended Mediterranean culture with Egyptian traditions and attracted settlers from throughout the known world.

The Library of Alexandria housed hundreds of thousands of scrolls and was the ancient world's greatest repository of knowledge, attracting scholars, philosophers, and poets from across the Mediterranean. The Pharos lighthouse stood over three hundred feet tall on the island of Pharos, guided Mediterranean shipping, and ranked as one of antiquity's Seven Wonders and greatest engineering feats.

Alexandria served as Cleopatra VII's royal residence and seat of power during the final century of Ptolemaic rule. It hosted her famous encounter with Julius Caesar and her alliance with Mark Antony. But Alexandria declined after the Roman Empire's conversion to Christianity. Pagan learning was suppressed, classical institutions were dismantled, and its role as a cosmopolitan intellectual center diminished. The city embodied the fusion of Greek and Egyptian civilizations.
